intro: Oakville is a town on the north shore of Lake Ontario between Toronto and Hamilton. In Bronte Creek Provincial Park, on its western edge, a white oak that likely germinated around 1685 spreads over an open meadow, one of the few trees in the region older than European settlement and an Ontario Heritage Tree since 2022. A reader sent us its photograph.

trees.name: The Heritage White Oak of Bronte Creek
trees.age_estimate: about 340 years (likely germinated around 1685, by the park's sign); about 300 by a reader's estimate

location.address: Bronte Creek Provincial Park, Oakville, Ontario

trees.story:
"It survived centuries of development intact," wrote the reader who sent us this white oak from Bronte Creek Provincial Park, between Oakville and Burlington on the shore of Lake Ontario.

The park's own sign, which the reader photographed too, says the same at greater length. The tree likely germinated around 1685, and it is one of the few left in the region that are older than European settlement. It was already standing when the Mississaugas and the British Crown signed the Head of the Lake Treaty in 1806, through the lumber boom of the 1800s and the farming and suburbs that followed. In 2022 it was recognised as an Ontario Heritage Tree.

The sign gives its measurements as well: 218 centimetres across the trunk at breast height, 684 centimetres round, 19 metres tall and a crown 32 metres wide. That is the shape a white oak takes when it grows in the open. The photograph shows a short, dark trunk dividing low into great grey limbs that reach out level over the grass, the crown far wider than the tree is tall.

The reader puts it at 300 years. A split-rail fence keeps a ring of ground clear around the roots. Stand by the sign and read the question it asks: how do you measure the value of a tree?
trees.how_to_recognise: Alone on a mown meadow: a broad white oak whose short dark trunk splits low into long level limbs, ringed by a wooden split-rail fence with a blue trilingual sign in front.

question_meta: The heritage white oak of Bronte Creek Provincial Park in Oakville, Ontario: about 340 years old, 684 cm round, and how to find it.
question_answer: The tree to see at Oakville is the Heritage White Oak of Bronte Creek, a white oak that likely germinated around 1685, on an open meadow in Bronte Creek Provincial Park.
question_context: Bronte Creek Provincial Park lies on the western edge of Oakville, between Oakville and Burlington, on the north shore of Lake Ontario. On an open meadow in the park stands a white oak, Quercus alba, that the park's own sign says likely germinated around 1685. That makes it one of the few trees left in the region older than European settlement, and in 2022 it was recognised as an Ontario Heritage Tree. The sign gives its size as 218 centimetres across the trunk at breast height, 684 centimetres round, 19 metres tall and 32 metres across the crown, the low, wide shape a white oak takes in the open. It stood through the Head of the Lake Treaty between the Mississaugas and the British Crown in 1806, the lumber boom of the 1800s and the farms and suburbs after it. A reader who sent us its photograph puts it at 300 years and says it survived centuries of development intact. A split-rail fence rings the roots, and the sign beside it asks how you measure the value of a tree.

faq.q: Where is the Heritage White Oak of Bronte Creek?
faq.a: On an open meadow in Bronte Creek Provincial Park, on the western edge of Oakville, Ontario, inside a split-rail fence with a sign beside it.

faq.q: How old is the Heritage White Oak of Bronte Creek?
faq.a: The park's sign says it likely germinated around 1685, which makes it about 340 years old. A reader puts it at about 300.

faq.q: Can I visit the Heritage White Oak of Bronte Creek?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in Bronte Creek Provincial Park, which charges a day-use fee; a low fence keeps visitors off the roots.
